blocks.text: A haemodialysis machine is a medical device that removes waste products and excess fluid from the blood and helps correct electrolyte and acid–base disturbances in patients with severe kidney dysfunction.
It works with a dialyzer, often called an artificial kidney, through which blood flows on one side of a semipermeable membrane while dialysate flows on the other.

items.text: Classification: Renal replacement therapy equipment.
Principle: Diffusion, ultrafiltration and, to a variable extent, convection.
Main indications: Selected patients with acute kidney injury, advanced chronic kidney disease or other conditions requiring renal replacement therapy.
Key identifying features: Control screen, blood pump, blood tubing, dialyzer connections, dialysate circuit and safety-monitoring systems.

blocks.text: OSCE distinction: The machine controls the dialysis process; the dialyzer contains the semipermeable membrane across which solutes and water are exchanged.

items.text: Removing accumulated urea and other small waste solutes.
Removing excess fluid in patients unable to maintain fluid balance.
Correcting selected electrolyte abnormalities, such as severe hyperkalaemia when dialysis is indicated.
Correcting acid–base disturbances, including severe metabolic acidosis in appropriate circumstances.
Providing renal replacement therapy for selected patients with acute kidney injury.
Long-term treatment for many patients with kidney failure who require maintenance dialysis.

blocks.text: The decision to initiate dialysis depends on the patient’s condition, complications, response to medical treatment and overall clinical goals—not on a single laboratory value alone.
A. Blood pump
Moves blood from the vascular access through the extracorporeal circuit and dialyzer at the prescribed flow rate.
B. Dialyzer
Contains a semipermeable membrane that allows selected solutes and water to move between blood and dialysate.
C. Extracorporeal blood circuit
Carries blood between the patient and dialyzer. Depending on the system, it includes arterial and venous lines, chambers and pressure-monitoring connections.
D. Dialysate preparation and delivery system
Prepares and delivers dialysate with the prescribed composition, flow and temperature. Water treatment and quality assurance are essential to safe dialysis.
E. Control panel
Allows trained staff to set and monitor treatment parameters, including blood flow, treatment time and prescribed fluid removal.
F. Safety-monitoring systems
Monitor parameters such as arterial and venous pressures, air in the venous line and dialysate conditions. Depending on the device, alarms can trigger protective responses.

items.text: Efficient removal of many small waste solutes.
Allows controlled removal of excess fluid.
Can correct selected electrolyte and acid–base disturbances.
Provides life-sustaining treatment for many patients with kidney failure.
Treatment parameters can be adjusted to the patient's clinical requirements.
Allows monitoring of treatment progress and selected circuit parameters.
Requires trained personnel, appropriate facilities and reliable water treatment.
Treatment is time-consuming and often requires repeated sessions.
Vascular access can be associated with infection, thrombosis, bleeding and other complications.
Rapid fluid or solute shifts can cause hypotension, cramps or dialysis disequilibrium in susceptible patients.
It does not fully replace the hormonal and metabolic functions of healthy kidneys.
Equipment failure, contaminated dialysate or circuit problems can create serious risks.
Some patients may not tolerate the prescribed treatment because of haemodynamic instability or other clinical factors.

blocks.title: Before dialysis begins, the trained dialysis team should:

items.text: Confirm the patient's identity, prescription and indication for treatment.
Review the patient's weight, fluid status, blood pressure, relevant laboratory results and clinical condition.
Verify the prescribed treatment duration, dialyzer, blood flow, dialysate composition and ultrafiltration target.
Check that the machine has passed required self-tests and that alarms and safety systems are operational.
Confirm the quality and suitability of the water supply and dialysate.
Inspect the dialyzer, blood tubing, connections and other consumables for integrity and expiry.
Assess the vascular access for patency, bleeding, infection and other complications.
Follow the prescribed anticoagulation plan, if applicable.
Record baseline observations and ensure emergency support is available.

blocks.text: Important safety precautions

items.text: Only trained personnel should set up, initiate or modify dialysis treatment.
Do not bypass alarms or use equipment that has failed required safety checks.
Air embolism, haemolysis, blood loss and dialysate-related electrolyte disturbances are potentially life-threatening.
Use only the prescribed dialysate composition and treatment settings.

If a patient develops chest pain, severe breathlessness, altered consciousness, significant hypotension or suspected haemolysis, initiate the appropriate emergency response and follow the machine-specific protocol.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to use it — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: This is an overview of the machine workflow for educational purposes, not a substitute for supervised dialysis training or the manufacturer's instructions.
Step 1: Verify the prescription
Confirm the patient, prescribed treatment and relevant clinical parameters. Establish baseline observations and review the vascular access.
Step 2: Check the machine
Complete the manufacturer-prescribed start-up checks and verify alarms, pressure monitoring, dialysate preparation and required quality-control checks.
Step 3: Prepare the extracorporeal circuit
Install the prescribed dialyzer and compatible blood tubing. Prime the circuit and remove air according to the approved device-specific procedure.
Step 4: Verify dialysate and settings
Confirm the prescribed dialysate composition, temperature, conductivity and other required parameters. Set the treatment according to the authorized prescription.
Step 5: Connect the patient
Using aseptic technique and the approved vascular-access procedure, connect the prepared circuit to the patient's access. Confirm secure connections before initiating treatment.
Step 6: Initiate and monitor treatment
Start treatment under the prescribed conditions. Monitor vital signs, access function, circuit pressures, alarms, fluid removal and the patient's symptoms.
Step 7: Complete and document

End treatment using the approved procedure, return blood when appropriate under the protocol, disconnect safely, assess the patient and access, and document the treatment delivered and any complications.

content_groups.group_title: Key parameters an examiner may ask about

rows: Blood flow rate
Determines the rate at which blood passes through the extracorporeal circuit.
Dialysate flow rate
Influences the exchange of solutes across the dialyzer membrane.
Ultrafiltration target
Specifies the intended fluid removal during treatment.
Arterial pressure
Reflects pressure in the blood line leading from the vascular access towards the pump.
Venous pressure
Reflects pressure in the return line from the dialyzer towards the patient.
Dialysate conductivity
Helps verify the ionic concentration of the dialysate mixture.
Dialysate temperature
Helps ensure dialysate is delivered within the prescribed safe range.
Treatment duration
Determines the planned duration of the dialysis session.

blocks.text: Exact targets depend on the patient's prescription, machine design and clinical circumstances.

There is no single absolute contraindication to all haemodialysis. The choice of renal replacement therapy depends on the patient's condition, urgency, vascular access, haemodynamic stability and treatment goals.

rows: Intradialytic hypotension
Dizziness, nausea, cramps or reduced blood pressure
Muscle cramps
Often associated with fluid shifts or ultrafiltration
Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
Neurological symptoms caused by rapid changes in solute balance, particularly in susceptible patients
Vascular-access infection
Redness, pain, discharge or systemic signs of infection
Vascular-access thrombosis
Reduced or absent access flow or a change in the expected thrill or bruit
Air embolism
Sudden respiratory, cardiovascular or neurological deterioration
Haemolysis
Potentially severe symptoms and abnormal blood appearance or laboratory findings
Blood loss
May occur with disconnection, circuit damage or other bleeding
Dialysate-related disturbance
May result from incorrect composition, temperature or water quality

blocks.text: Suspected air embolism, haemolysis, major blood loss or severe cardiovascular instability requires immediate emergency action according to the local protocol and machine instructions.
A haemodialysis machine does not have one universal “normal reading.” Its parameters must match the patient's prescription and the device's specifications.
Potentially reassuring findings

items.text: Machine self-tests and required quality-control checks are satisfactory.
Dialysate parameters remain within the prescribed and device-approved limits.
Blood circuit connections are secure and the circuit is free of visible air.
Pressures and alarms are consistent with the patient's access and circuit conditions.
The patient remains clinically stable during treatment.

blocks.text: Concerning findings

items.text: Recurrent pressure alarms or unexpected pressure changes.
Air detected in the venous circuit.
Unexpectedly abnormal conductivity or dialysate temperature.
Visible blood leakage, tubing damage or a loose connection.
Significant hypotension, chest pain, breathlessness or altered consciousness.

blocks.text: “The haemodialysis machine is connected to the extracorporeal blood circuit and prescribed dialyzer. I would confirm that the safety checks and dialysate parameters are satisfactory, verify the treatment prescription, and monitor circuit pressures, ultrafiltration and the patient's clinical condition throughout the session. Any abnormal alarm or clinical deterioration would be assessed and escalated immediately.”

items.text: Children require individualized dialysis prescriptions based on body size, clinical needs and the modality being used.
Use appropriately sized dialyzers, blood tubing and vascular access.
The extracorporeal blood volume can be significant relative to a small child's circulating blood volume.
Monitor temperature, blood pressure, fluid balance and electrolytes closely.
Neonates and infants require specialist renal support and equipment suitable for their size.
Caregivers should receive appropriate education regarding vascular access, treatment schedules and warning signs.
Pediatric dialysis should be delivered by a team experienced in renal replacement therapy for children.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the principle of haemodialysis?
Haemodialysis removes waste solutes and excess water from blood using diffusion and ultrafiltration across a semipermeable membrane, with convection contributing in some systems.
Q2. What is a dialyzer?
It is the component containing the semipermeable membrane across which blood and dialysate exchange solutes and water.
Q3. What are the major components of the machine?
The blood pump, extracorporeal blood circuit, dialyzer connections, dialysate delivery system, control panel and safety-monitoring systems.
Q4. What is ultrafiltration?
Ultrafiltration is the movement of water across the dialyzer membrane driven by a pressure gradient. It is used to remove excess fluid during dialysis.
Q5. Why is dialysate conductivity monitored?
Conductivity helps assess whether the dialysate mixture has the expected ionic concentration. Abnormal readings may indicate a preparation or delivery problem.
Q6. What is the purpose of the air detector?
It detects air in the venous blood line and triggers protective responses intended to reduce the risk of air entering the patient's circulation.
Q7. What are common complications during haemodialysis?
Intradialytic hypotension, muscle cramps, vascular-access problems, bleeding, infection and, rarely, serious circuit-related complications such as air embolism or haemolysis.
Q8. What would you do if a patient suddenly became breathless and hypotensive during dialysis?

I would call for urgent assistance, assess airway, breathing and circulation, and initiate emergency management according to the clinical situation and dialysis-unit protocol. I would assess for serious treatment-related complications and follow the machine-specific emergency procedure.
Common mistakes

items.text: Confusing the machine with the dialyzer.
Failing to check the treatment prescription.
Ignoring machine self-test failures or quality-control issues.
Failing to prime the circuit correctly.
Bypassing alarms or ignoring unexpected pressure changes.
Overlooking the patient's vascular access.
Assuming that a normal machine display guarantees patient stability.
Failing to monitor fluid removal and haemodynamic status.

blocks.text: Examiner tips

items.text: Explain the roles of diffusion and ultrafiltration.
Identify the blood pump, dialyzer, blood circuit and dialysate system.
Mention the importance of water quality and dialysate conductivity.
Explain the function of air detection and pressure monitoring.
State that the machine must be set according to an authorized prescription.
Emphasize patient monitoring throughout the session.

blocks.text: Practice station
Scenario

You are in a renal unit and are shown a haemodialysis machine prepared for a patient with kidney failure. The examiner asks you to identify the machine, explain its principle and describe the essential safety checks before treatment.
Your tasks

items.text: Identify the instrument and state its purpose.
Name four major components.
Explain the roles of diffusion and ultrafiltration.
State four important safety checks.
Describe your response to an air alarm or sudden patient deterioration.
